steps: Let T = n P D_1 on D_nat = H_n cap Dom(D_1), where P is the S-symmetriser onto H_n and D_1 shifts theta_1 to theta_1 - i pi/3.
Since J = D(tau_1) is a unitary involution with JP = PJ = P, one has T Psi = (n/2) P (D_1 + J D_1 J) Psi for every Psi in D_nat (identity (3.1)).
Because J Psi = Psi on H_n, the paper's identity (3.2), T Psi = (n/2)(D_1 + J D_1 J) Psi, holds iff Phi = D_1 Psi + J D_1 Psi already lies in H_n.
Phi = D_1 Psi + J D_1 Psi is automatically invariant under D(tau_1), and under D(tau_j) for j >= 3 since those commute with D_1 and J; so Phi in H_n reduces to D(tau_2)-invariance.
Since D(tau_2) D_1 Psi = D_1 Psi, identity (3.2) holds for Psi in D_nat with n >= 3 iff D(rho_3) D_1 Psi = D(rho_2) D_1 Psi, where rho_2 = tau_1 and rho_3 = tau_2 tau_1.

To refute (3.2) take the entire S-symmetric vector Psi_n = prod_{i<j} h(theta_i - theta_j) prod_i exp(-theta_i^2/2) with h(u)/h(-u) = S(u); Psi_n lies in D_nat and each shift D_k Psi_n is direct evaluation.

With theta_1, theta_2, theta_4, ..., theta_n fixed and distinct, the ratio R(x) = D(rho_3)D_1 Psi_n / D(rho_2)D_1 Psi_n at theta_3 = x equals exp(i pi (x - theta_2)/3)(L + o(1)) with L finite and nonzero.
If (3.2) held for Psi_n, real-analyticity would force R(x) = 1 for all large x, so L + o(1) = exp(-i pi (x - theta_2)/3), whose right side does not converge; contradiction.
Therefore (3.2) fails for every n >= 3, the symmetrised shift (D_1 + J D_1 J)/2 does not commute with P, and Section 3 of the paper studies the wrong operator for n >= 3.

traps.text: D_sym = (D_1 + J D_1 J)/2 commutes with J, hence with P, so the outer projection can be dropped and T = n D_sym on H_n for every n.
traps.why: P is generated by all D(tau_k); commuting with D(tau_1) says nothing about D(tau_2) when n >= 3.

traps.text: Slots 3,...,n are spectators, only the pair (theta_1, theta_2) is touched, so the n = 2 analysis of (3.2) is uniform in n.
traps.why: T = sum_k D(rho_k) D_1 shifts every slot; the tau_2 constraint exists only for n >= 3 and is exactly where (3.2) breaks.

steps: Corollary 3.21 asks for an i pi/3-periodic meromorphic Q with Q(nu) = P(nu) Q(-nu), where P is i pi/3-periodic meromorphic on C with P(nu) P(-nu) = 1.
The relation P(nu) P(-nu) = 1 shows P is not identically zero and gives P(-nu) = 1/P(nu) as an identity of meromorphic functions.
Put Q = 1 + P; then Q(-nu) = 1 + P(-nu) = 1 + 1/P(nu) = (1 + P(nu))/P(nu).
Multiplying by P(nu) gives P(nu) Q(-nu) = 1 + P(nu) = Q(nu), so Q = 1 + P solves Q(nu) = P(nu) Q(-nu) as meromorphic functions.
Q = 1 + P is i pi/3-periodic because P is, and is nonzero unless P is identically -1, in which case the odd function Q = sinh(6 nu) is a nonzero periodic solution.
Hence for every admissible P, whatever the winding number of F with P = F(exp(6 nu)), nonzero i pi/3-periodic solutions Q of Q(nu)/Q(-nu) = P(nu) exist.
Consequently the chain odd winding number => no periodic Q => no nonzero S-symmetric solution => m_n = 0 of Theorem 3.29 fails at its first step, for every n.

traps.text: Write Q = F^{1/2} H with H(x) = H(1/x); if F has odd winding number then F^{1/2} is not single-valued on C*, hence no single-valued Q exists.
traps.why: H may carry the same monodromy -1 as F^{1/2}; e.g. F = x^{2m+1}, G = 1 + x^{2m+1} is a polynomial solution.

traps.text: Since nonzero periodic Q always exist, the lattice problem has solutions and therefore m_n > 0, i.e. T is not essentially self-adjoint.
traps.why: The pointwise lattice problem is not shown equivalent to ker(T*+1) in either direction; its solutions say nothing about Dom(T*).

steps: Let U_kappa be multiplication by exp(i kappa (theta_1 + ... + theta_n)) on L^2(R^n); it is unitary and commutes with every D(sigma) because the rapidity sum is permutation invariant.
Averaging over S_n, the unitary U_kappa commutes with the S-symmetriser P and maps H_n onto H_n, with inverse U_{-kappa}.
In Fourier variables U_kappa translates t by kappa(1,...,1), so the weight e^{pi t_1/3} gains a factor e^{pi kappa/3}: D_1 U_kappa = e^{kappa pi/3} U_kappa D_1 and U_kappa Dom(D_1) = Dom(D_1).
Combining with T = n P D_1 on D_nat, U_kappa D_nat = D_nat and U_kappa^* T U_kappa = e^{kappa pi/3} T, so <U_kappa Psi, T U_kappa Psi> = e^{kappa pi/3} <Psi, T Psi>.
For a fixed unit vector Psi in D_nat, U_kappa Psi is again a unit vector in D_nat whose T-expectation e^{kappa pi/3}<Psi, T Psi> tends to 0 as kappa -> -infinity.
Therefore inf{<Psi, T Psi> : Psi in D_nat, ||Psi|| = 1} = 0 on every H_n, so T >= epsilon fails for every epsilon > 0.
In particular T is not >= 1 on any H_n and cannot itself be the positive dominating operator T_DF >= 1 demanded by the Driessler-Frohlich theorem.

traps.text: Since T >= 0, the operator 1 + T satisfies 1 + T >= 1 and therefore serves as the Driessler-Frohlich dominating operator for phi~ and phi~'.
traps.why: 1 + T violates DF bound (1) for chi'_1(g) already on H_1 (w(lambda) = 1 + lambda has lambda w(lambda) -> 0).

traps.text: Since inf T = 0 is attained by no vector, T has a spectral gap above 0 on each H_n that can be used to prove m_n = 0.
traps.why: The dilation shows spec(T_F) = [0, infinity); there is no gap to exploit.

steps: On H_1 = L^2(R), D = Delta^{1/6} is multiplication by e^{pi t/3} in Fourier space, and chi'_1(g) = sqrt(2 pi |R|) M_{b_g} D^{-1} with b_g continuous and not identically zero.
Suppose a positive self-adjoint T_DF has H_1-part w(D) with lambda w(lambda) -> 0 as lambda -> 0, and ||B psi|| <= c ||T_DF psi|| on a core, where B restricts to chi'_1(g) on H_1.
Closing B, the bound ||B xi|| <= c ||T_DF xi|| extends from the core to every xi in Dom(T_DF) cap Dom(B).

Take phi with Fourier transform supported in [-M, M], eta_Lambda = e^{-i Lambda theta} phi and xi_Lambda = D eta_Lambda; the spectral measure of D in xi_Lambda lies in [e^{-pi(M+Lambda)/3}, e^{pi(M-Lambda)/3}].
By the spectral theorem ||T_DF xi_Lambda|| = ||(lambda w)(D) eta_Lambda|| <= s(Lambda) ||phi||, where s(Lambda), the sup of lambda w(lambda) over 0 < lambda <= e^{pi(M-Lambda)/3}, tends to 0.
For the same xi_Lambda = D eta_Lambda, ||B xi_Lambda|| >= sqrt(2 pi |R|) ||b_g eta_Lambda|| >= sqrt(2 pi |R|) delta ||1_I phi|| > 0, since |eta_Lambda| = |phi| and |b_g| >= delta on I.
The extended bound would force a fixed positive constant to be <= c s(Lambda) for all large Lambda, impossible as s(Lambda) -> 0; so DF bound (1) fails for chi'_1(g).
Hence neither T (w(lambda) = lambda) nor 1 + T (w(lambda) = 1 + lambda) can dominate phi~'(g), already on the one-particle space H_1.

traps.text: The obstruction is structural: no function w(T) can dominate both chi_1(f) and chi'_1(g), since a function of one shift never controls the inverse shift.
traps.why: False: w(lambda) = 1 + lambda + 1/lambda >= max(lambda, 1/lambda) dominates both D and D^{-1} on H_1 (referee F1).

For Phi, Psi in H_n, = n = n

= n , because P is an orthogonal projection with P Phi = Phi.
Hence Phi in H_n lies in ker(T*+1) iff n <Phi, D_1 Psi> + <Phi, Psi> = 0 for every test vector Psi in H_n cap Dom(D_1) = D_nat.
Suppose Phi in ker(T*+1) also lies in Dom(D_1); then Phi is in H_n cap Dom(D_1) = D_nat and is itself an admissible test vector Psi.
Taking Psi = Phi gives n <Phi, D_1 Phi> + ||Phi||^2 = 0, and D_1 >= 0 makes both terms nonnegative, so Phi = 0.
Therefore every nonzero deficiency vector Phi of T lies outside Dom(D_1): e^{pi t_1/3} times the Fourier transform of Phi is not square integrable.
So for a nonzero deficiency vector the shifted function Phi(theta_1 - i pi/3, ...) is not an L^2 function, and a pointwise shift equation for Phi cannot be read off term by term.

traps.text: Reading (T*+1)Phi = 0 through the pointwise formula (3.2) gives a three-term lattice recursion in nu, so deficiency vectors are exactly the L^2 lattice solutions.
traps.why: T* has no pointwise formula; the conversion needs analyticity and strip L^2 bounds that deficiency vectors provably lack.

traps.text: The condition holds for test vectors in H_n cap Dom(D_1), so it holds for all Psi in Dom(D_1), giving Phi in ker(n D_1 + 1) = {0} and m_n = 0.
traps.why: Test vectors are restricted to the S-symmetric part; extending to all of Dom(D_1) is unjustified and would trivially kill the deficiency.

steps: Every sigma in S_n factors uniquely as sigma = rho_{sigma(1)} o sigma-bar, where rho_k = tau_{k-1} ... tau_1 sends 1 to k and sigma-bar fixes 1.
For sigma-bar fixing 1, D(sigma-bar) = 1 tensor V acts only on slots 2,...,n, so D(sigma-bar) commutes with D_1, the imaginary shift in slot 1.
For Psi in D_nat, D(sigma-bar) D_1 Psi = D_1 D(sigma-bar) Psi = D_1 Psi, because Psi is S-symmetric.
Hence D(sigma) D_1 Psi = D(rho_{sigma(1)}) D_1 Psi for every sigma in S_n and every Psi in D_nat.
Each k in {1,...,n} equals sigma(1) for exactly (n-1)! permutations, so summing over S_n gives n! P D_1 Psi = (n-1)! sum_k D(rho_k) D_1 Psi.
Therefore T Psi = n P D_1 Psi = sum_{k=1}^n D(rho_k) D_1 Psi for Psi in D_nat: the compression T shifts every slot k, with multipliers coupling slot k to slots 1,...,k-1.

traps.text: Since T = n P D_1 P contains only the slot-1 shift, T acts on theta_1 alone and the deficiency problem reduces to a one-variable recursion for every n.
traps.why: The projection P spreads D_1 to every slot; for n >= 3 there is no relative variable and the formal equation is an n-shift equation.

steps: For f in L^2(R) and psi in H_n, ||z^dag(f) psi||^2 = (n+1)<f(x)psi, P_{n+1}(f(x)psi)>, a sum over S_{n+1} grouped into the n+1 cosets {sigma : sigma(1) = k}.
Terms in the coset sigma(1) = 1 all equal <f,f>||psi||^2, and in each coset k >= 2 the exchange relation moves theta_k to slot 1, cancelling every S-factor except S(theta_k - theta_1).
Hence ||z^dag(f)psi||^2 = ||f||^2||psi||^2 + n int conj(f(theta)) f(theta') S(theta' - theta) conj(psi(theta',Theta)) psi(theta,Theta), the exchange identity.
Writing S = -1 + eps with eps = S + 1, the -1 part equals -||z(f)psi||^2, so ||z^dag(f)psi||^2 = ||f||^2||psi||^2 - ||z(f)psi||^2 + E with E the eps-integral.

For supp f in an interval I of length l < pi/6 with centre theta_0, expanding eps(theta' - theta) binomially about theta_0 gives E = sum_k e_k sum_j C(k,j)(-1)^{k-j} <z(f_j)psi, z(f_{k-j})psi>, f_j = (theta - theta_0)^j f.
Since ||f_j|| <= (l/2)^j ||f|| and ||z(h)psi|| <= a_n(l)||h|| ||psi||, each pairing is at most a_n^2 (l/2)^k ||f||^2||psi||^2, and summing binomials gives |E| <= kappa(l) a_n(l)^2 ||f||^2||psi||^2.
Dropping the nonpositive term -||z(f)psi||^2 gives ||z^dag(f)psi||^2 <= (1 + kappa(l) a_n(l)^2)||f||^2||psi||^2, i.e. b_n(l)^2 <= 1 + kappa(l) a_n(l)^2.
Since a_{n+1}(l) = b_n(l) by adjointness, a_{n+1}^2 <= 1 + kappa(l) a_n^2, and iterating from a_0 = 0 gives a_n(l)^2 <= 1 + kappa + ... + kappa^{n-1}.
If kappa(l) < 1 the geometric sum is below 1/(1 - kappa(l)), so ||z^dag(f)|| = ||z(f)|| <= ||f||_2/sqrt(1 - kappa(l)) for supp f of length l, uniformly in particle number.

traps.text: Bound |S| <= 1 inside the integral to get ||z^dag(f)psi||^2 <= (n+1)||f||^2||psi||^2 and hence a global n-independent bound on z^dag(f).
traps.why: That only gives sqrt(n+1) growth; a global CAR-type bound failed, and n-uniformity needs S near -1 on short supports.

traps.text: The same Taylor expansion of eps works for any support length l, so the local bound extends to f supported on intervals of any length.
traps.why: eps has radius of convergence exactly pi/6 (pole at -i pi/6); kappa(l) diverges for l >= pi/6.

steps: Write S(t) = P_+(s)/P_-(s) with s = sinh t and P_pm(s) = prod_c (s pm i c), c in {sqrt3/2, -1/2, -1}; S has poles where sinh t = i c and zeros where sinh t = -i c.
For t = x + i y, sinh t = sinh x cos y + i cosh x sin y; if |y| < pi/6 then cos y > 0, so sinh t is purely imaginary only when x = 0.
On x = 0 with |y| < pi/6, sinh t = i sin y with |sin y| < 1/2, while every c has |c| >= 1/2, so sinh t = pm i c has no solution in the strip.
Hence S is analytic and zero-free on the open strip |Im t| < pi/6, and eps = S + 1 is analytic on the disc |t| < pi/6.
At t = -i pi/6, sinh t = -i/2 matches the factor c = -1/2 of P_-, a simple pole since cosh(-i pi/6) = sqrt3/2 is nonzero; so the Taylor radius of eps at 0 is exactly pi/6.
Since eps is analytic on |t| <= rho for any rho < pi/6, Cauchy's estimate gives |e_k| <= M(rho)/rho^k, so kappa(l) = sum_k |e_k| l^k is finite for every l < pi/6.

traps.text: For |y| < pi/6 one has |sinh t| < 1/2 throughout the strip, so sinh t = pm i c with |c| >= 1/2 is impossible.
traps.why: |sinh(x + i y)| is unbounded in x; the argument must use that sinh t is purely imaginary only on x = 0.

traps.text: Because |S| = 1 on the real axis, the Taylor series of eps also converges for l = 0.6 > pi/6, so kappa(0.6) is finite.
traps.why: Boundedness on R is irrelevant; the pole at -i pi/6 fixes the radius at pi/6 and kappa diverges beyond it.

steps: In ||z^dag(f)psi||^2 = ||f||^2||psi||^2 - ||u||^2 + E with u = z(f)psi, the j = 0 and j = k terms of the moment expansion of E pair z(f_k)psi against u.
By the parity conj(e_k) = (-1)^k e_k of the Taylor coefficients of eps = S + 1, those two terms combine to 2 Re[e_k <z(f_k)psi, u>] = 2 Re<z(e_k f_k)psi, u>.
Summing over k with g = eps(theta - theta_0) f = sum_k e_k f_k in L^2 gives E = 2 Re<v, u> + R, with v = z(g)psi and R the terms 1 <= j <= k-1.
Completing the square in H_{n-1}, -||u||^2 + 2 Re<v,u> = -||u - v||^2 + ||v||^2, hence ||z^dag(f)psi||^2 <= ||f||^2||psi||^2 + ||v||^2 + |R|.
Because |eps(theta - theta_0)| <= kappa(l/2) on I, ||g|| <= kappa(l/2)||f|| and so ||v||^2 = ||z(g)psi||^2 <= a_n^2 kappa(l/2)^2 ||f||^2||psi||^2.
For the remainder, sum_{j=1}^{k-1} C(k,j) = 2^k - 2 gives |R| <= (kappa(l) - 2 kappa(l/2)) a_n^2 ||f||^2||psi||^2, the first-order |e_1| terms cancelling exactly.
Adding the two bounds, b_n(l)^2 <= 1 + kappa'(l) a_n(l)^2 with kappa'(l) = kappa(l) - 2 kappa(l/2) + kappa(l/2)^2, and iteration gives a_n^2 <= 1/(1 - kappa'(l)) when kappa'(l) < 1.
Numerically kappa'(1/32) = 0.00716 against kappa(1/32) = 0.1224, so c'(1/32) < 1.0036, and the admissible cell length rises from about 0.1803 to about 0.2604.

traps.text: Since ||u - v||^2 >= 0 the term ||v||^2 can be dropped as well, leaving ||z^dag(f)psi||^2 <= ||f||^2||psi||^2 + |R|.
traps.why: Completing the square produces +||v||^2; only -||u - v||^2 is nonpositive and may be dropped.

traps.text: Using the largest admissible cell length l close to 0.2604 minimises the energy-bounded constant, since fewer cells are needed to cover the rapidity window.
traps.why: c'(l) blows up as l approaches its threshold; the product c'(l)^2 N_cells is best near l = 1/8 among tabulated values.

steps: A vector Psi in ran P_E, with P_E the spectral projection of H = dGamma(cosh) onto H <= E, has each n-particle component supported in {sum_i cosh theta_i <= E}.
Since each cosh theta_i >= 1, every rapidity of every n >= 1 component of Psi in ran P_E lies in the window W_E = [-arccosh(E), arccosh(E)].
Split f = f_W + f_out with f_W = f 1_{W_E}; in the polarised exchange identity every integral containing f_out vanishes, so ||z^dag(f)Psi||^2 = ||z^dag(f_W)Psi||^2 + ||f_out||^2 ||Psi||^2.
Cover W_E by N = max(1, ceil(2 arccosh(E)/l)) disjoint cells I_m of length <= l, and write f_W = sum_m f_m with f_m = f 1_{I_m}.
The local bound on each cell and the triangle inequality give ||z^dag(f_W)Psi|| <= c(l) sum_m ||f_m||_2 <= c(l) sqrt(N) ||f_W||_2 by Cauchy-Schwarz over disjoint supports.
Combining with the splitting and c(l)^2 N >= 1 yields ||z^dag(f)Psi||^2 <= c(l)^2 N (||f_W||^2 + ||f_out||^2) = c(l)^2 N ||f||_2^2 for unit Psi in ran P_E.
Hence ||z^dag(f) P_E|| <= c(l) sqrt(N_cells(E)) ||f||_2 for every f in L^2(R), a loss of order sqrt(log E) because arccosh(E) <= log(2E).

traps.text: At E = 1 the window W_E is the single point 0, so ceil(0/l) = 0 cells are needed and ||z^dag(f) P_1|| = 0.
traps.why: P_1 contains the vacuum projection and ||z^dag(f)Omega|| = ||f||; the cell count must be max(1, .).

traps.text: The sqrt(log E) growth is intrinsic to this S-matrix: sup over unit f of ||z^dag(f) P_E|| really grows like sqrt(log E).
traps.why: It is a loss of the triangle-inequality method; for S = -1 the true value is 1, and O(1) for this S is open.

steps: The collapse identity (K) states F_min(z + i pi) F_min(z) B_r(z) = mu^2 with B_r(z) = r(z + i pi/3) r(z + 2i pi/3), as an identity of meromorphic functions.
Since F_min(. + i pi) is zero-free on |Im w| < pi, (K) can be solved as F_min(w) = mu^2 / [F_min(w + i pi) B_r(w)] on the collar strip |Im w| < pi/6.
Evaluating this formula at w and at -w and dividing gives [F_min(w)/F_min(-w)] [F_min(w + i pi)/F_min(-w + i pi)] [B_r(w)/B_r(-w)] = 1.
From log F_min(z) = int_0^inf a0(t)[1 - cos((z - i pi)t)] dt, F_min(w + i pi) depends on w only through cos(wt), so F_min(w + i pi) = F_min(-w + i pi).
Since r is even, B_r(-w) = r(-w + i pi/3) r(-w + 2i pi/3) = r(w - i pi/3) r(w - 2i pi/3) = A_r(w).
The rational identity A_r(w)/B_r(w) = S(w) in s = sinh w then gives B_r(w)/B_r(-w) = 1/S(w), hence F_min(w) = S(w) F_min(-w): Watson's relation, derived from (K).
Because R_ba = -R_ab and r is even, K_ab(w) = K_ba(-w); with Watson's relation, P_ab = f K_ab (f = F_min/mu) satisfies P_ab(w) = S(w) P_ba(-w) for all labels.

traps.text: Prove (K) by a Fourier transform on the boundary line Im z = pi, where both factors are read off directly from the integral representation.
traps.why: There z + i pi sits on the edge Im = 2 pi of the representation's strip; the valid proof uses the interior centre line Im z = pi/2.

traps.text: By the same evenness of the integrand, F_min itself is even, F_min(w) = F_min(-w), on the real axis.
traps.why: Only F_min(w + i pi) is even; F_min(w)/F_min(-w) = S(w), and F_min has a simple zero at 0 with F_min'(0) = -i sqrt3 mu^2.

steps: The cubic crossed kernel is F_cross(x,y) = F0 lambda^3 sum_{a,b,c} w_a w_b w_c P_ab(y - x) P_ac(y + i pi + i0) P_bc(x + i pi + i0), with P_ab = f K_ab and f = F_min/mu.
Near x = 0 only the crossed factor P_bc(x + i pi) can be singular, with a simple pole exactly for (b,c) in {(+,-),(-,+)}, of residues -i rho L/mu and +i rho L/mu.
Using w_+ w_- = 1, Res_{x=0} F_cross = F0 lambda^3 (i rho L/mu) sum_a w_a [P_{a-}(y) P_{a+}(y + i pi) - P_{a+}(y) P_{a-}(y + i pi)].
For each label a, r even and 2 pi i-periodic give K_{a-}(y) K_{a+}(y + i pi) = B_r(y) and K_{a+}(y) K_{a-}(y + i pi) = A_r(y).
By (K) divided by mu^2, f(y) f(y + i pi) B_r(y) = 1, so P_{a-}(y)P_{a+}(y + i pi) = 1 and P_{a+}(y)P_{a-}(y + i pi) = A_r(y)/B_r(y) = S(y).
Hence the bracket equals 1 - S(y) for every label a, and Res_{x=0} F_cross = F0 lambda^3 (i rho L/mu)(g + 1/g + h)(1 - S(y)) with h = -sqrt(2 - sqrt3).
Since rho L = 1/sqrt3 and lambda^2 = sqrt3 mu give lambda^2 rho L/mu = 1, Res_{x=0} F_cross = i F1 (1 - S(y)) with F1 = F0 lambda (g + 1/g - sqrt(2 - sqrt3)).

traps.text: The outgoing factor P_ab(y - x) also contributes a pole on the line y = x, from r(w + i pi d/3) with d = +-1, so y = x is a third singular line.
traps.why: The simple zero of f at 0 cancels that simple pole of K_ab; the line y = x is removable.

traps.text: At the corner x = y = 0 both simple poles meet, so F_cross has a genuine 1/(xy) double pole with coefficient 2 i F1.
traps.why: Terms with both poles have outgoing factor f(y - x) with f(0) = 0, so the 1/(xy) coefficient vanishes: Phi(0,0) = 0.

steps: The rotation table satisfies R_ba = -R_ab and r is even, so K_ba(-w) = prod_{d in R_ab} r(-w - i pi d/3) = K_ab(w) for all labels.
With Watson's relation f(w)/f(-w) = S(w), the factors P_ab(w) = f(w) K_ab(w) satisfy P_ab(w) = S(w) P_ba(-w) for all labels a, b.
Swapping the outgoing slots of F_cross relabels a <-> b and x <-> y: F_cross(y,x) = F0 lambda^3 sum w_a w_b w_c P_ba(x - y) P_ac(y + i pi) P_bc(x + i pi).
Substituting P_ab(y - x) = S(y - x) P_ba(x - y), the label-independent factor S(y - x) leaves the sum, so F_cross(x,y) = S(y - x) F_cross(y,x).
Hence the outgoing S-symmetriser (P_{2,S} psi)(x,y) = [psi(x,y) + S(y - x) psi(y,x)]/2 acts as the identity on the full crossed kernel F_cross.
Taking residues in F_cross(x,y) = S(y - x) F_cross(y,x) and using S(x)S(-x) = 1 gives R_2(x) = S(-x) R_1(x): the two pole terms differ by the unimodular Watson factor.

traps.text: Therefore the regular remainder G = F_cross - chi(x)R_1(y)/x - chi(y)R_2(x)/y is S-symmetric as well, and symmetrising G first is vacuous.
traps.why: False (v3 error): P_{2,S} G = G + D/2 with a nonzero bounded divided-difference defect D from the cutoff pole terms.

traps.text: The same argument works in the engine convention psi(a,b) = S(a - b) psi(b,a), so F_cross is S-symmetric in either exchange convention.
traps.why: In that convention P_{2,S} F_cross = (1 + S(x - y)^2)/2 F_cross, not F_cross; the convention is load-bearing.

steps: For real t write S = prod_c b_c with b_c(t) = (sinh t + i c)/(sinh t - i c), c in {sqrt3/2, -1/2, -1}, each factor unimodular on R.
Then b_c - 1 = 2ic/(sinh t - ic), so |b_c(t) - 1| = 2|c|/sqrt(sinh^2 t + c^2) for real t.
Since sinh^2 t + c^2 = cosh^2 t - (1 - c^2) >= c^2 cosh^2 t whenever |c| <= 1, each factor obeys |b_c(t) - 1| <= 2 sech t.
For unimodular factors |prod b_c - 1| <= sum_c |b_c - 1|, so |S(t) - 1| <= 6 sech t for all real t.
Also (log b_c)'(t) = -2ic cosh t/(sinh^2 t + c^2), and the same lower bounds on sinh^2 t + c^2 give |S'(t)| <= (6 + 4/sqrt3) sech t.
Adding and using sech t <= 2 e^{-|t|}, |S(t) - 1| + |S'(t)| <= (12 + 4/sqrt3) sech t <= 29 e^{-|t|} on R.
For the residue R_1(y) = i F1 (1 - S(y)), |R_1(y)| + |R_1'(y)| = |F1| (|1 - S(y)| + |S'(y)|) <= 29 |F1| e^{-|y|}, which is the residue decay CUB (3).

traps.text: With the residues and their decay proved from (K), the cubic ESA theorem no longer depends on any identification of the kernel with the Bullough-Dodd field.
traps.why: Whether the explicit kernel is the correct connected form factor of the collar field (tower identification) is still an unproved input.

steps: The minimal form factor is log F(z) = int_0^inf a0(t)[1 - cos((z - i pi)t)] dt on 0 < Im z < 2 pi, with log mu = int_0^inf a0(t) dt.
For 0 < Im z < pi both z and z + i pi lie in that strip, so log F(z + i pi) + log F(z) - 2 log mu = -int_0^inf a0(t)[cos(zt) + cos((z - i pi)t)] dt.
By cos A + cos B = 2 cos((A+B)/2) cos((A-B)/2), this equals -2 int_0^inf a0(t) cosh(pi t/2) cos((z - i pi/2)t) dt.
Hence (K) on the centre line z = x + i pi/2 is equivalent to log B(x + i pi/2) = 2 int_0^inf a0(t) cosh(pi t/2) cos(xt) dt, with B(z) = r(z + i pi/3) r(z + 2i pi/3).
The two factors of B(x + i pi/2) are complex conjugates, so B(x + i pi/2) = (c+1)(c+1/2)/[c(c + sqrt3/2)] > 0 with c = cosh x, and its logarithm is real.
Writing each factor cosh x + cos(phi) through L_beta(x) = log(1 - 2 cos(beta) e^{-x} + e^{-2x}) gives log B(x + i pi/2) = L_pi + L_{2pi/3} - L_{pi/2} - L_{5pi/6}.

Since int_0^inf L_beta(x) cos(tx) dx = 1/t^2 - pi cosh((pi - beta)t)/(t sinh(pi t)) and the signed multiplicities sum to zero, the cosine transform of log B(x + i pi/2) is pi(C_3 + C_1 - C_2 - 1)/(t sinh(pi t)).
The Chebyshev identity (1 - H) C_3 = C_3 + C_1 - C_2 - 1, with C_j = cosh(j pi t/6), identifies this transform with pi a0(t) cosh(pi t/2).
Fourier cosine inversion, valid since log B(x + i pi/2) is even, continuous and O(e^{-|x|}), returns the centre-line identity, so (K) holds on Im z = pi/2.
Both sides of (K) are analytic and zero-free on 0 < Im z < pi, so the identity theorem extends (K) from the centre line to the whole strip.

traps.text: Set Im z = 0 in the same computation to obtain (K) directly on the real axis from the integral representation.
traps.why: At Im z = 0 the point z is outside the convergence strip 0 < Im z < 2 pi; real-axis F is defined only by continuation.

traps.text: Each L_beta transform contains a 1/t^2 term, so the transform of log B is not integrable at t = 0 and Fourier inversion cannot be applied.
traps.why: The four 1/t^2 terms cancel exactly because the multiplicities +1, +1, -1, -1 sum to zero.

steps: At b = 1/sqrt3, substituting t = pi s in the Brazhnikov-Lukyanov integrand gives the numerator 4 cosh(pi s/6) sinh(pi s/12) sinh(pi s/4) = 2 cosh(pi s/6)(C_2 - C_1).
By product-to-sum identities 2 cosh(pi s/6)(C_2 - C_1) = C_3 + C_1 - C_2 - 1, which equals (1 - H(s)) C_3 by the definition of H.
Dividing by sinh(pi s) cosh(pi s/2) = sinh(pi s) C_3 gives 4 [BL integrand](pi s)/s = (1 - H(s))/(s sinh(pi s)) = a0(s), the collar weight function.
Hence log R(theta) = -int_0^inf a0(s) cosh(s(pi - i theta)) ds = -int_0^inf a0(s) cos((theta + i pi)s) ds for the BL minimal form factor R.
Since log F(-theta) = int_0^inf a0(s)[1 - cos((-theta - i pi)s)] ds and cosine is even, log R(theta) = log F(-theta) - log mu.
Therefore R(theta) = f(-theta) = F_min(-theta)/mu, convergent on -2 pi < Im theta < 0, the reflection of the collar strip 0 < Im z < 2 pi.

traps.text: Since both are minimal form factors of the same S-matrix, R(theta) = f(theta) without reflection.
traps.why: The integrals give f(-theta); the convergence strips -2 pi < Im < 0 versus 0 < Im < 2 pi confirm the reflection.

steps: Assume J_1(g) = g + 1/g + h = 0 with h = -sqrt(2 - sqrt3), i.e. g = e^{+-5 i pi/12}, and inductively J_k(.; g) = 0 identically for 1 <= k <= n-1.
For generic z_2, ..., z_n, phi(x_1) = J_n(z; g) is a rational function of x_1 = e^{z_1} whose only possible singularities in C* are simple poles at x_1 = y x_w with y^6 = 1.
Because J_n is symmetric in (z_1, ..., z_n), it suffices to prove regularity on d_12 = z_1 - z_2 in {0, i pi/3, 2i pi/3, i pi}.
At d_12 = 0, J_n = N/(x_1 - x_2) with N antisymmetric under x_1 <-> x_2, so N vanishes on the diagonal and the singularity is removable.
At d_12 = i pi/3 the pairs (0,0) and (-,+) contribute residue coefficient rho_r(h^2 - r(0)) = 0, since r(0) = 2 - sqrt3 = h^2; so J_n is regular there.
At d_12 = 2i pi/3 the residue equals rho_r h prod_{v>=3} r(u_0 - z_v) J_{n-1}(u_0, z_3, ...), which vanishes by the induction hypothesis.
At d_12 = i pi the residue is proportional to J_{n-2}(z_3, ..., z_n), zero by induction for n >= 3, while for n = 2 the bracket prod B - prod B is 1 - 1 = 0.
So phi has no poles in C*; as x_1 -> 0 or infinity every r-factor tends to 1, so phi tends to J_1(g) J_{n-1} = 0 at both ends.
A rational function of x_1 with no poles on the Riemann sphere is constant, here 0; hence J_n(.; g) = 0 identically, completing the induction for every n >= 1.

traps.text: Since J_1 = J_2 = 0 at g_0 and a numerical check gives |J_n(g_0)| < 1e-11 for n <= 6, the collapse J_n(g_0) = 0 holds for all n.
traps.why: That was the v1 gap: n <= 2 proved plus numerics is not a proof; the residue induction is needed.

traps.text: Hence the tower singles out a = 0 as the unique collapse point, so the BL parameter a is uniquely fixed by the collar tower.
traps.why: The tower collapses on the whole orbit 2 sqrt6 Z union (-5/sqrt6 + 2 sqrt6 Z); a is fixed only modulo a dihedral group.

steps: The label swap sigma exchanging + and - satisfies R_{sigma a, sigma b} = -R_ab, so with r even K(sigma a, sigma b; d) = K(a, b; -d), and w_{sigma a}(g) = w_a(1/g).
Relabelling every term of the label sum by sigma gives J_n(z; 1/g) = J_n(-z; g) for all n, all g in C* and all z.
Delta = J_n(.; g) - J_n(.; 1/g) is symmetric and rational in x_1 = e^{z_1}, with possible simple poles only on d_12 in {0, i pi/3, 2i pi/3, i pi} up to symmetry.
The residues of Delta at d_12 = 2i pi/3 and i pi are multiples of J_{n-1}(g) - J_{n-1}(1/g) and J_{n-2}(g) - J_{n-2}(1/g), zero by induction, and d_12 = 0, i pi/3 are regular.
As x_1 -> 0 or infinity, Delta -> J_1(g)J_{n-1}(g) - J_1(1/g)J_{n-1}(1/g) = 0, since J_1(g) = J_1(1/g); so Delta vanishes identically and J_n(z; g) = J_n(z; 1/g).
Hence g -> J_n(z; g) is a palindromic Laurent polynomial of degree n, i.e. a monic degree-n polynomial P_n in J_1(g) = g + 1/g + h.
With the collapse theorem P_n(z; 0) = 0, so J_1 divides J_n, and for |g| = 1 the towers at g and conj(g) coincide, making g = +-1 the fixed points.

traps.text: Since J_n(z; 1/g) = J_n(-z; g) and J_n is not even in z, the towers at g and 1/g are genuinely different.
traps.why: The induction shows J_n(z; g) = J_n(z; 1/g) = J_n(-z; g) identically.

traps.text: The point g = 1 has no distinguished role in the collar family; every unimodular g gives a different field.
traps.why: False v2 claim: the family depends only on cos(arg g), and g = +-1 are fixed points of g -> 1/g.

steps: The kinematic residue axiom gives Res_{eta_1 = theta_1} K_(r,k) = -i (1 - Phi_{theta_{>=2}, eta_{>=2}}(theta_1)) K_(r-1,k-1) for the connected kernel K_(r,k).
For s matched pairs the first residue carries Phi_{theta_{>=2},eta_{>=2}}(z_1) = [prod_{a=2}^s S(theta_a - z_1) S(z_1 - eta_a)] Phi_{theta',eta'}(z_1), with theta', eta' the unmatched variables.
That factor is holomorphic in eta_2, ..., eta_s near the real axis because S has no real poles, so the later residues at eta_a = theta_a pass through it unchanged.
After all s residues theta_a = eta_a = z_a, and the bracket becomes prod_a S(z_a - z_1) S(z_1 - z_a) = 1 by unitarity S(t)S(-t) = 1.
Hence the iterated residue is (-i)^s prod_{p=1}^s (1 - Phi_{theta',eta'}(z_p)) K_(r-s,k-s)(theta'; eta'): each matched pair keeps 1 - Phi over the unmatched particles only.
If all particles are matched, r - s = k - s = 0, then Phi_{();()} = 1 and every factor vanishes, so the fully matched iterated residue is zero; e.g. F_2(theta + i pi, eta) has no kinematic pole.

traps.text: Since the double residue of K_(2,2) vanishes, the single-delta part of W_(2,2) vanishes as well, and W_(2,2) has no matched-pair contribution.
traps.why: The single residue keeps 1 - Phi over the unmatched pair, which is nonzero; that single-delta part X_1 grows linearly.

steps: With the mu-delta delta = 2 pi delta_L, the upper prescription splits each Cauchy factor as 1/(x - i0) = PV(1/x) + i pi delta_L(x) = PV(1/x) + delta(x)/2.
Expanding over incoming variables, a term with s injective contractions eta_{sigma(p)} = theta_p carries (i pi)^s delta_L^s times the s-fold iterated kinematic residue of K_(r,k).
The iterated residue equals (-i)^s prod_p (1 - Phi(z_p)) K_(r-s,k-s), so the s-pair delta part is (1/2)^s prod_p delta(eta_p, theta_p)(1 - Phi(theta_p)) K^(0)_(r-s,k-s) summed over patterns.
Lifted to operators, the s-pair delta part of W_(r'+s,k'+s) is the nested insertion N_s[g, K^(0)_(r',k')] with pair density g = (1 - Phi)/2.
On H_n with t = n - k' spectators, N_s[g, B] = c P_m[(B (x) I_t) M_{e_s}]P_n, where e_s is the degree-s elementary symmetric polynomial in f(y_q) = g(y_q) Psi(y_q).
Summing over s uses sum_s e_s = prod_q (1 + f(y_q)), and with Phi = 1/Psi one gets 1 + g Psi = 1 + (Psi - 1)/2 = (1 + Psi)/2 = omega.
Hence sum_s W_(r'+s,k'+s)[K^{+,[s]}] on H_n equals c P_m[(K^(0)_(r',k') (x) I_t) M_{prod_q omega(y_q)}]P_n, a spectator dressing with |omega| <= 1 pointwise.

traps.text: With the PV residual, the matched-pair delta parts sum to W^{Psi}[K^(0)] - W[K^(0)], i.e. every spectator picks up the full phase Psi.
traps.why: False: the multiplier is omega = (1 + Psi)/2; the difference W^{Psi} - W^{omega} is nonzero with O(1) relative size.

traps.text: Since |prod omega| <= 1, ||(B (x) I) M_{prod omega}|| <= ||B||, so the resummed lift is bounded by the undressed lift for every residual kernel.
traps.why: omega depends on (theta', eta'), making it a Schur-type product; the bound needs the binomial-average argument and only holds for L^2-bounded B.

steps: Let u, g, f_2, ..., f_n be unit vectors in L^2(R, dmu) with pairwise disjoint supports, a = u (x) f_2 (x) ... (x) f_n and Phi = sqrt(n!) P_n a.
Since P_n is the orthogonal projection (1/n!) sum_pi D(pi), <Phi, Phi> = n! <a, P_n a> = sum_{pi in S_n} <a, D(pi) a>.
Each D(pi) a is a unimodular function times the tensor product with slots permuted, so its support meets supp a in positive measure only when every slot keeps its factor, i.e. pi = id.
Hence only pi = id contributes and ||Phi||^2 = <a, a> = 1 for the S-symmetrised product state Phi = sqrt(n!) P_n a.
With b = g (x) f_2 (x) ... (x) f_n and Psi = sqrt(n!) P_n b, the same support argument together with supp u disjoint from supp g gives <Phi, Psi> = 0.

traps.text: Since P_n is a projection, ||P_n a|| = ||a|| = 1, so Phi = P_n a is already normalised without the factor sqrt(n!).
traps.why: a is not S-symmetric, so P_n a has norm 1/sqrt(n!) here; the disjoint supports kill all non-identity terms.

steps: By the delta decomposition, W_(3,3)[K^+_(3,3)] = X_2 + N_1[(1 - Phi)/2, K^(0)_(2,2)] + W_(3,3)[K^(0)_(3,3)], the triple-delta part vanishing because fully matched residues vanish.
On orthogonal S-symmetrised product states Phi_n, Psi_n with narrow disjoint windows, the double-delta piece has <Phi_n, X_2 Psi_n> = int conj(u) B g e_2(nubar_2, ..., nubar_n).
On the explicit family this gives |<Phi_n, X_2 Psi_n>| >= C(n-1,2) |nu0|^2 |B0| m_ug/2, a lower bound quadratic in the particle number n.
The PV pieces are suppressed by the window width w_n = eps delta^2 n^{-5/2}: the f_q are real and each PV is odd, giving |P_2| = O(n^{-1/2}) and |Q_2| = O(n^{1/2}).
The double-PV piece obeys |P_3| <= (3/16) M^(3) C_sigma eps^2 m_ug n^2, which is below |nu0|^2 |B0| m_ug n^2/16 once eps is chosen small.
With the degree-2 and degree-4 contributions O(n), |<Phi_n, A^{<=6} Psi_n>| >= n^2 |nu0|^2 |B0| m_ug/8 for all large n.
Since Phi_n, Psi_n have energy spread below 1 and energy N_n ~ n cosh(y0), some shell block Z_{M'} A^{<=6} Z_{N'} with bounded M' - N' has norm >= c N_n^2.
This violates the adaptive budget ||Z_m A Z_n|| <= C (n+2) log(n+2) v_{m-n} for every C, so the cubic method does not extend degree by degree to the degree-6 truncation.

traps.text: Therefore the full Bullough-Dodd field A(h) violates the adaptive cutoff criterion CUT (7).
traps.why: The theorem concerns the truncation; the full-field matrix element contains higher-degree PV residuals that are not controlled.

traps.text: Since the degree-4 truncation only has a linear lower bound, it satisfies the (n+2) log(n+2) budget of CUT (7).
traps.why: A lower bound proves nothing about the upper bound; whether A^{<=4} satisfies CUT (7) is open.

steps: Let T: L^2(J) -> L^2(I x I') have kernel chi(theta - eta) R(u,eta)/(theta - eta + i0) + G(theta,u;eta), with int(I cap J) nonempty, R bounded with bounded d_eta R, and G in L^2.
The G part is Hilbert-Schmidt, hence compact, and splitting R(u,eta) = R(u,theta) + (R(u,eta) - R(u,theta)) makes the second piece a bounded, hence Hilbert-Schmidt, kernel on the bounded cells.
So T differs by a compact operator from psi -> R(u,theta) (k * psi)(theta), the convolution with k(x) = chi(x)/(x + i0) multiplied by R(u,theta).
The symbol of k is -i pi(sgn xi + 1) + o(1), which tends to the nonzero limit m_* = -2 pi i as xi -> +infinity.
For phi in C_c^inf(int(I cap J)) the vectors psi_j = phi e^{i j eta} are weakly null with ||psi_j|| = ||phi||, and ||k * psi_j - m_* psi_j|| -> 0 by Plancherel.
Hence ||T psi_j||^2 -> |m_*|^2 int_{I'} int_I |R(u,theta)|^2 |phi(theta)|^2, which is positive for suitable phi when R(u,theta) is nonzero on a set of positive measure.
A compact operator maps weakly null sequences to norm-null ones, so T is not compact, hence not nuclear: a Cauchy part with nonzero residue is never nuclear on overlapping cells.

traps.text: For the +i0 prescription the symbol vanishes as xi -> -infinity, so the +i0 Cauchy part is compact on bounded cells.
traps.why: Non-compactness needs a nonzero limit in only one direction; as xi -> +infinity the symbol tends to -2 pi i.

traps.text: Shrinking the cells to length l makes the Cauchy part nuclear on each diagonal cell with nuclear norm O(l), so the cell-summed nuclear bound (Lemma B) survives.
traps.why: The argument works on every cell meeting the pole, however small; Lemma B fails from degree (2,1) on.

steps: Let I, J be intervals with |I| = l, and K in L^2(I x J) with d_x K in L^2, x in I; set a = ||K||_2 and b = (l/pi)||d_x K||_2.
In the cosine basis e_0 = l^{-1/2}, e_n = (2/l)^{1/2} cos(pi n (x - x_0)/l) of L^2(I), every f in H^1(I) satisfies sum_n (pi n/l)^2 |<e_n, f>|^2 = ||f'||^2, by even reflection.
With k_n(y) = <e_n, K(., y)> one has K = sum_n e_n (x) k_n, so the trace norm obeys ||K||_1 <= sum_n ||k_n||.
By Parseval sum_n ||k_n||^2 = a^2, and by the cosine-basis derivative identity sum_n n^2 ||k_n||^2 = b^2.
Cauchy-Schwarz with weights 1 + n^2 gives sum_n ||k_n|| <= (sum_{n>=0} (1 + n^2)^{-1})^{1/2} (a^2 + b^2)^{1/2}.
Since sum_{n>=0} (1 + n^2)^{-1} = (1 + pi coth pi)/2, ||K||_1 <= C_0 (a^2 + b^2)^{1/2} with C_0 = ((1 + pi coth pi)/2)^{1/2} = 1.4411: K is nuclear from L^2(J) to L^2(I).

traps.text: The same bound with first derivatives in each variable controls the projective norm of kernels in q >= 3 variables.
traps.why: For q variables the cosine argument needs mixed derivatives of order q - 1 in q - 1 variables.

traps.text: Since each cell is nuclear, occupation-pattern orthogonality sums cell contributions in l^2, improving the N_cells^{r+k} power in the lift bound.
traps.why: Inputs with different patterns reach the same output; the power N^{r+k} is attained in the hard-core toy model.

steps: For distinct outgoing theta_1, theta_2, partial fractions in eta_1 then eta_2 write K_(2,2) as sum_{a,b} [N/(d_a d_b)](eta_1 - theta_a)^{-1}(eta_2 - theta_b)^{-1} plus terms with at most one Cauchy factor.
The coefficient of each double Cauchy term is the iterated residue Res_{eta_2 = theta_b} Res_{eta_1 = theta_a} K_(2,2).
For a = b the contraction is non-injective: S(0) = -1 forces K_(2,2) = 0 on eta_1 = eta_2 where it is finite, so this coefficient vanishes.
For a != b the iterated residue is (-i)^2 Omega prod_p (1 - Phi_{();()}(z_p)) K_(0,0), which vanishes because Phi_{();()} = 1 when no particle is unmatched.
Hence K_(2,2) is a regular part plus single-Cauchy terms with coefficients -i Omega (1 - Phi_{theta_b; eta_j'}) K_(1,1), where K_(1,1) itself has no kinematic pole.
In general the j-pair coefficient (-i)^j Omega prod_p (1 - Phi) K_(r-j,k-j) vanishes when j = r = k, so j_max(r,r) = r - 1 and two-pair terms first appear at degrees (3,2) and (2,3).

traps.text: Since (2,2) carries at most one Cauchy pair, the j-pair bilinear bound gives an O(p) bound for the (2,2) block directly.
traps.why: The single-pair coefficient couples the pair variable to the spectators, so the product-kernel bound does not apply; O(p) is only an inference.

traps.text: So the two-pair Cauchy mechanism is closed from degree (2,2) onward.
traps.why: Wrong: (2,2) has no two-pair term, but (3,2), (2,3) and higher do, and these are the genuine n^2 candidates.

steps: Let C be Hilbert-Schmidt on L^2(R), X bounded, T = int C(theta,eta) z^dag(theta) X z(eta), and {I} a sharp partition of the creator variable into cells of length <= l.
On each cell take the singular value decomposition 1_I C = sum_i s_i |a_i><b_i| with a_i orthonormal in L^2(I) and b_i orthonormal in L^2(R).
Then for phi in H_{p'} and psi in H_p, <phi, T psi> = sum_{I,i} s_i <z(a_i) phi, X z(b_i) psi>.
Each a_i is supported in a cell of length <= l, so the local ZF bound gives ||z(a_i)|| <= c'(l) uniformly in particle number.
Cauchy-Schwarz in i gives sum_i s_i ||z(b_i) psi|| <= ||1_I C||_HS (sum_i ||z(b_i) psi||^2)^{1/2}.
Bessel for ZF annihilators gives sum_i ||z(b_i) psi||^2 = p int sum_i |<b_i, psi(., x)>|^2 dx <= p ||psi||^2 on H_p.
Hence ||T on H_p|| <= c'(l) ||X|| sqrt(p) sum_I ||1_I C||_HS <= c'(l) ||X|| sqrt(p) sqrt(#I) ||C||_HS, one factor sqrt(p) instead of sqrt(p(p+1)).

traps.text: Applying the same bound pair by pair to the j-pair coefficient (-i)^j Omega prod_p(1 - Phi) K_(r-j,k-j) gives (A p)^j times the smooth-part bound.
traps.why: That coefficient does not factorise over pairs and spectators; a separated-coefficient hypothesis is needed and was unstated.

steps: Define phi_2(x) = F_2(x + i pi, 0) = F0 lambda^2 J_2(x + i pi) F_min(x + i pi)/mu, so that F_2(theta + i pi, eta) = phi_2(theta - eta).
On the line Im z = pi, log F_min(x + i pi) = int_0^inf a0(t)(1 - cos xt) dt with a0 >= 0 and both a0 and t a0 integrable.
Hence 1 <= F_min(x + i pi) <= mu^2, its log-derivative is bounded by int t a0(t) dt, and by Riemann-Lebesgue F_min(x + i pi) -> mu with derivative -> 0 as |x| -> infinity.
J_2(x + i pi) is rational in u = e^x, and its only possible poles on (0, infinity) are simple poles at u = 1 from the (+,-) and (-,+) label terms.
Both of those terms have weight w_+ w_- = 1 and their residues at x = 0 are negatives of each other, so the singularity is removable for every g.
Each factor r(x + iy) tends to 1 as u -> 0 or infinity, so J_2(x + i pi) is a bounded rational function on R tending to (g + 1/g + h)^2 = J_c^2.
Therefore phi_2 is real-analytic and in C^1_b(R), with phi_2(x) -> F0 lambda^2 J_c^2 and phi_2'(x) -> 0 as |x| -> infinity.

traps.text: Global boundedness of phi_2 and phi_2' follows directly from the kinematic residue axiom and the pole structure (POLE).
traps.why: Those give absence of the pole and local analyticity only; global C^1_b bounds need the F_min and J_2 asymptotics.

steps: Assume Omega is cyclic and separating for M_0, and that translations by x in closure(W_L) map M_0 into itself, with Tomita operator S_M.
Borchers' theorem on the two lightlike rays gives Delta_M^{it} U(s a_pm) Delta_M^{-it} = U(e^{-+2 pi t} s a_pm) and J_M U(x) J_M = U(-x).
Hence Delta_M^{it} acts on the momentum P_mu as a Lorentz boost and J_M P_mu J_M = P_mu, so both commute with the mass operator P^2 = P_mu P^mu.
Since P^2 = 0 on H_0, m^2 on H_1 and >= 4m^2 on H_{>=2}, the projection P_1 is a spectral projection of P^2, so Delta_M and J_M commute with P_1.

V(t) = Delta_M^{it} U(Lambda(2 pi t))^* commutes with translations and boosts, so irreducibility on H_1 gives Delta_M restricted to H_1 = e^c Delta_1 and J_M restricted to H_1 = omega J_1, |omega| = 1.
Polynomial approximation gives S_M f^+ = (conj f)^+, while directly S_1 f^+ = conj f^+(. + i pi) = (conj f)^+; so omega e^{c/2} = 1, forcing e^c = 1 and omega = 1.
Therefore on H_1 the modular data are free, Delta_1^{it} psi(theta) = psi(theta - 2 pi t) and J_1 psi = conj psi, and P_1 S_M is contained in S_1 P_1 with S_1 psi = conj psi(. + i pi).

traps.text: Since the H_1 modular data are free, the modular data of (M_0, Omega) are the second-quantised free data Gamma(Delta_1), Gamma(J_1) on all of Fock space.
traps.why: Borchers pins the modular data only on H_1; nothing constrains the H_{>=2} components.

steps: Suppose Omega is separating for M_0 at S = S_{1/2}; then S_M sends phi(f_1)phi(f_2)phi(f_3)Omega to phi(f_3)phi(f_2)phi(f_1)Omega for real f_j in C_c^inf(W_L), and P_1 S_M is contained in S_1 P_1.
Hence g = P_1 phi(f_1)phi(f_2)phi(f_3)Omega lies in Dom(S_1) and S_1 g = g~ := P_1 phi(f_3)phi(f_2)phi(f_1)Omega.
Contracting with the ZF relations, g = a_12 f_3^+ + a_23 f_1^+ + f_2^+ I_13 with I_13(u) = int F(theta) S(u - theta) d theta and F = f_1^- f_3^+.
Continuing I_13 upward, the poles of S(u - theta) at theta = u - i pi/3 and u - 2i pi/3 cross the real contour, adding 2 pi i R_1 F(u - i pi/3) and 2 pi i R_2 F(u - 2i pi/3).
By uniqueness of H^2 continuation from the real line, the continuation of g equals g^cont built from these terms, so S_1 g = conj g^cont(. + i pi).
Crossing S(t + i pi - theta) = S(theta - t) turns the regular integral into I_31, and with R_2 = -R_1 one gets conj g^cont(t + i pi) - g~(t) = D(t) = -4 pi i r f_2^+(t) Im F(t + i pi/3).
Here r = 90 - 52 sqrt3 is nonzero, so S_1 g = g~ forces Im F(t + i pi/3) f_2^+(t) = 0 for almost every real t.
For product test functions with ordered supports, Im F(t + i pi/3) = 0 would force F(w + i pi/3) = F(w) and exponential decay contradicting Paley-Wiener, so D is not identically zero.
This contradiction shows Omega is not separating for Lechner's wedge algebra M_0 at S = S_{1/2}; the obstruction is the residue of S at i pi/3.

traps.text: Continue I_13 to Im u = pi by moving u under the integral sign as for a pole-free S, giving conj g^cont(t + i pi) = g~(t) and no defect.
traps.why: The poles of S at i pi/3 and 2 i pi/3 cross the contour; their residues produce exactly the nonzero defect D.

traps.text: Since Omega is not separating, E = [M_0' Omega] is the vacuum projection, so M_0' = C 1 and M_0 = B(H).
traps.why: Only P_1 E = 0 is proved; whether E equals the vacuum projection is open.

steps: The degree-2 Tomita map T_2 sends phi(f_1)...phi(f_k)Omega, k <= 2, to phi(conj f_k)...phi(conj f_1)Omega, extended antilinearly.
Take the candidate S_Gamma = (conjugation on H_0) + S_1 + S_2 with (S_2 Psi)(a,b) = conj Psi(b + i pi, a + i pi), the joint continuation.
J_2 Psi(a,b) = conj Psi(b,a) preserves H_2 because conj S(a - b) = S(b - a) on R, and Delta_2 = Gamma(Delta_1) preserves H_2 because S depends only on b - a.

For phi(f_1)phi(f_2)Omega = a_12 Omega + Psi, the joint continuation moves each f_j^+ inside its H^2 strip and leaves S(b - a) unchanged, so S_2 Psi is the H_2 part of phi(conj f_2)phi(conj f_1)Omega.
Hence T_2 is contained in the closed operator S_Gamma, so the degree-2 Tomita map is well defined and closable.
This argument used only |S| = 1, dependence on theta_2 - theta_1, conj S(theta) = S(-theta) and f^+ in H^2; strip poles and crossing never entered.
So degree-2 separation holds for every such S, including S_{1/2} where Omega is not separating: it is no test, and the first S_{1/2}-sensitive degree is the cubic (1,3) split.

traps.text: Hence Omega is separating on H_0 + H_1 + H_2 for M_0 at S_{1/2}, a partial positive result toward separation.
traps.why: It holds for every admissible S regardless of separation; in the operator sense separation fails already on H_0 + H_1.

traps.text: By Lechner's theorem Omega is separating for the ZF wedge algebra M_0, so (M_0, Omega) has modular data and degree 3 will pass as well.
traps.why: Lechner's result needs S bounded analytic on the strip; S_{1/2} has poles at i pi/3 and 2 i pi/3, and Omega is not separating.

steps: Let E be the projection onto the closure of M_0' Omega; then E lies in M_0, E Omega = Omega, and E is not 1 because Omega is not separating for M_0.
E commutes with all translations and boosts, by a Schwarz-reflection argument on lightlike rays together with boost invariance of M_0' and Omega.
Hence E commutes with P_1, and P_1 E P_1 commutes with the irreducible one-particle representation, so P_1 E is either 0 or P_1.
If P_1 E = P_1, the reduced algebra E M_0 E on EH has Omega cyclic and separating and is covariant, so its Tomita operator satisfies P_1 S_E contained in S_1 P_1.
Then S_1 g = g~ for the one-particle component of the cubic vector phi(f_1)phi(f_2)phi(f_3)Omega, contradicting the nonzero residue defect D; hence P_1 E = 0.
So A = 1 - E is a nonzero projection in M_0 with A Omega = 0 and A >= P_1.
Its compression satisfies P_{<=1} A P_{<=1} = P_1, nonzero, so Omega is not separating even for the compressed family on H_0 + H_1.

traps.text: By irreducibility P_1 E must equal P_1, since E Omega = Omega and E contains the one-particle vectors f^+ generated from Omega.
traps.why: f^+ comes from M_0 Omega, not M_0' Omega; the dichotomy is resolved to P_1 E = 0 via the residue defect.

steps: At degree one the collar kernels are K_(1,0)(theta) = H_h(P(theta)) F_1 and K_(0,1)(eta) = H_h(-P(eta)) F_1, with F_1 = F0 lambda J_c and J_c = g + 1/g + w_0.
For real smearing h, conj H_h(k) = H_h(-k), so conj K_(1,0)(eta) = H_h(-P(eta)) conj F_1.
Hence K_(0,1) = conj K_(1,0) on the set where H_h(P(.)) is nonzero if and only if F_1 is real.
Since F0, lambda = -sqrt(sqrt3 mu) and w_0 = -sqrt(2 - sqrt3) are real, F_1 is real if and only if q = g + 1/g is real.
Writing g = |g| e^{i alpha}, Im q = (|g| - 1/|g|) sin(alpha), which vanishes if and only if |g| = 1 or sin(alpha) = 0, i.e. g in R union S^1.
So for F0 real and nonzero and h with H_h not vanishing on the mass shell, the degree-one Hermiticity K_(0,1) = conj K_(1,0) holds exactly for g in (R union S^1) minus {0}.

traps.text: Reflection of the real smearing h gives Hermiticity of every collar kernel for all complex g, so A_{<=2}(h) is symmetric for every g.
traps.why: Only claimed in the record; Hermiticity fails outside R union S^1, e.g. at g = 1.3 e^{0.71 i}.

steps: A_{<=2}(h) is symmetric on D_fin, and its only nonzero off-diagonal blocks A_mn = P_m A P_n have |m - n| in {1, 2} with ||A_mn|| <= L (min(m,n) + 2).
Let v be in ker(A* - i) with a_n = ||v_n||; since each block is bounded, (A* v)_m = sum_{|n-m|<=2} A_mn v_n = i v_m for every m.
Pairing with v_m, summing over m <= N and taking imaginary parts, the symmetric part with m, n <= N is real, so sum_{n<=N} a_n^2 = Im of the crossing terms with m <= N < n.
The crossing pairs are (N-1,N+1), (N,N+1), (N,N+2), each block of norm <= L(N+2), and 2ab <= a^2 + b^2 gives sum_{n<=N} a_n^2 <= L(N+2) sum_{j=N-1}^{N+2} a_j^2.
If v is nonzero, the left side exceeds ||v||^2/2 for N >= N_0, so sum_{j=N-1}^{N+2} a_j^2 >= ||v||^2/(2L(N+2)) for all such N.
Summing over N >= N_0, the right sides diverge like a harmonic series while the left sides total at most 4||v||^2; hence v = 0, and likewise ker(A* + i) = 0.
A densely defined symmetric operator with both deficiency spaces zero is essentially self-adjoint, so A_{<=2}(h) is essentially self-adjoint on D_fin.

traps.text: Each block A_mn is bounded, so A_{<=2}(h) is a bounded symmetric operator and therefore self-adjoint.
traps.why: The block norms grow linearly in n, so A_{<=2}(h) is unbounded; the deficiency argument is needed.

traps.text: The same argument proves ESA for any field whose blocks grow like (n+2)^2 at bounded transfer.
traps.why: The argument needs sum over N of 1/c_N to diverge; for quadratic growth the series converges and no contradiction arises.

steps: Assume A = A_{<=3}(h) is symmetric on finite-energy vectors D_E and its shell blocks satisfy ||Z_m A Z_n|| <= C_1(h)(min(m,n) + 2) v'_{|m-n|} with v' summable, and likewise for d_0 h.
The blocks of A (H+1)^{-1} are then at most 2 C_1 v'_{|m-n|}, so the Schur test gives ||A psi|| <= C_2 ||(H+1) psi|| on D_E.
Since e^{itH} z^dag(theta) e^{-itH} = e^{it cosh theta} z^dag(theta), one has [H, W_(r,k)[K]] = W_(r,k)[(E_out - E_in) K] as forms on D_E.
In the collar kernels h enters only through H_h(P_out - P_in), and k^0 H_h(k) = H_{i d_0 h}(k), so [H, A_{<=3}(h)] = A_{<=3}(i d_0 h) up to sign.
With y_n = (n+2)^{1/2}||Z_n psi||, the block bound for d_0 h, (min(m,n)+2) <= sqrt((m+2)(n+2)) and Young's inequality give |<psi, [H,A] psi>| <= C ||(H+1)^{1/2} psi||^2.
D_E is a core for H, so Nelson's commutator theorem with N = H + 1 gives essential self-adjointness of A_{<=3}(h) on D_E and on every core of H.

traps.text: Symmetry of A_{<=3}(h) on D_E follows from the symmetric bounded-energy realisation of the cubic part Y_3 alone.
traps.why: That covers only Y_3; the (1,1), (2,0), (3,0) pieces need Hermiticity, which fails for non-unimodular complex g.

traps.text: The same Nelson argument then gives essential self-adjointness of every finite truncation A_{<=D}(h).
traps.why: Already the degree-6 truncation has shell blocks >= c N^2, so the relative bound by H + 1 fails.
